name: LLM (ChatGPT) news headline sentiment

origin.source_title: Can ChatGPT Forecast Stock Price Movements? Return Predictability and Large Language Models (arXiv 2304.07619)

how_it_works.simple: You ask a chatbot whether each news headline is good or bad for the company. Then you buy companies with good news and sell those with bad news for a day.
how_it_works.analogy: Like having a fast reader scan the morning paper and tell you which shops just got good or bad reviews.
how_it_works.precise: Prompt GPT-4 with each firm headline to score it as good, bad or unknown for the stock; form an equal-weighted daily long-short portfolio from positive and negative scores. Most of the measured skill is the non-tradable initial reaction; the tradable part is the next-day drift.

rule: For headlines released after the close (or overnight), score each with the LLM; at the next open buy all firms scored positive and short all scored negative, equal weighted, and close at the next close. Require at least two firms per leg.
data_needed: Timestamped firm-level news headlines (RavenPack or Dow Jones, typically paid)
LLM API access with a knowledge cutoff before the test period
economic_rationale: Investors underreact to news, especially for small caps and negative news, and limits to arbitrage slow the correction (Lopez-Lira and Tang).
why_it_might_fail: Lopez-Lira and Tang report the Sharpe fell from 6.54 in 2021Q4 to 1.22 in early 2024 as LLM use spread, and 20 bps round-trip costs make it unprofitable. Glasserman and Lin (2023) show in-sample LLM backtests mix lookahead bias with a distraction effect from company names.

reported_results.notes: Read in the arXiv PDF. GPT-4 (gpt-4-0314, training data to September 2021) overnight-news drift strategy, 34 bps per day before costs. At 10 bps round trip the Sharpe falls to 1.29; 20 bps makes it unprofitable. Turnover about 190 percent per day. Yearly Sharpe: 6.54 (2021Q4), 3.68 (2022), 2.33 (2023), 1.22 (Jan-May 2024).

Anonymized headlines outperform original headlines in-sample, so the distraction effect outweighs lookahead bias; out-of-sample lookahead is not a concern but distraction remains. Recommends stripping company names from prompts.

post_publication_evidence: The authors' own updated sample shows steady decay (Sharpe 6.54 to 1.22 by mid-2024). Any backtest using a model whose training data overlaps the test window is contaminated; Glasserman and Lin propose anonymizing entities.

implementations.notes: Open LLM sentiment pipelines; not the authors' code.

relevance.reason: The same headline-scoring approach could be applied to macro and central bank news for FX, if the model's knowledge cutoff predates the test window.
